name: Cancer
introduction: is the Crab, sent to distract Hercules during his fight with the Hydra. It is the faintest of the zodiac constellations, a dim upside-down Y between Gemini and Leo, best found on dark northern spring evenings. About 2,000 years ago, the Sun stood in Cancer at the June solstice, which gave the Tropic of Cancer its name.

sections.title: What makes it special
paragraphs: At its heart lies the Beehive Cluster, M44, also known as Praesepe, the Manger: a swarm of about a thousand stars, roughly 600 light-years away, visible to the naked eye as a misty patch. In 1609, Galileo was among the first to see through a telescope that it consists of many stars.
Two stars flanking the cluster, [Asellus Borealis](hip:42806) and [Asellus Australis](hip:42911), are the “donkeys” feeding at the manger.

sections.title: Notable stars
paragraphs: [Tarf](hip:40526) is the brightest star, an orange giant about 320 light-years away. [Acubens](hip:44066), the crab’s claw, is a multiple star. Asellus Australis lies almost on the ecliptic, so the Moon often passes in front of it.
The faint star [Copernicus](id:cns5-2182), also known as 55 Cancri, has five known planets. The innermost, 55 Cancri e, is a scorching super-Earth that may be covered by an ocean of lava.

sections.title: Beyond the stars
paragraphs: Cancer also contains the open cluster M67, one of the oldest known, about four billion years old, nearly as old as the Sun. Its stars are a valuable laboratory for understanding how Sun-like stars age.
